Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette: Alejandro Hernandez, a 45-year-old European-American journalist, had always been drawn to high-stakes reporting. His most recent assignment, however, would prove to be his most harrowing experience yet. While investigating human trafficking in Eastern Europe, Alejandro was kidnapped and held captive for three days by his subjects. The memories of those 72 hours remained etched in his mind like a scar. Alejandro recalled the feeling of being bound and gagged, unable to move or speak. His captors would occasionally enter the room, their loud footsteps echoing off the walls, making him flinch with each creak of the floorboards. The smell of cheap alcohol wafted from their breath, making his stomach turn. Even now, the scent of booze made Alejandro's gut twist into knots. Physical touch, too, had become a trigger; a gentle pat on the back or an accidental brush of arms would send him recoiling. As he sat in captivity, Alejandro became convinced that every sound signaled his impending execution. The creaks and groans of the old building seemed to take on menacing tones – each one a potential harbinger of doom. This hypervigilance persisted long after his rescue. Alejandro found himself perpetually "on guard," waiting for the next shoe to drop. Loud noises still made him jump, his heart racing as he frantically scanned his surroundings for potential threats. Sleep eluded Alejandro, haunted by the unrelenting replay of memories from those three days. His mind would get stuck on a particular moment – the feeling of helplessness, the stench of sweat and fear – and play it back on an infinite loop. He'd try to distract himself with work or TV, but his brain seemed to have developed a mind of its own. The memories would force their way into his consciousness at inopportune moments, like during meetings or while driving. Remembering the event still brought back the same terror he felt at the time – his breath caught in his throat, his vision blurring. Alejandro's wife, Sarah, began to notice changes in him. He'd become withdrawn and irritable, snapping at her for no reason. She'd try to offer comfort, but Alejandro would recoil from physical touch, unable to explain why. His neck pain, a nagging companion since the ordeal, had worsened, as if his body was still tensed for impact. As a journalist, Alejandro's instincts told him to push through, to not let the experience define him. But he couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly "on edge." Colleagues began to comment on his jumpy demeanor, and editors started questioning his ability to cover high-pressure assignments. The job that had once brought him such fulfillment now felt like a minefield. One evening, as Alejandro was working late in his home office, Sarah approached him with tears in her eyes. She couldn't take the distance between them anymore; she wanted the old Alejandro back. For the first time since his captivity, Alejandro broke down, confessing to the nightmares and the crippling fear that had taken hold of his life. It was then that he realized he needed help – not just for himself, but for those around him who were suffering alongside him. Alejandro's decision to seek therapy marked a tentative step toward reclaiming control over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't help but wonder if it was possible to silence the perpetual alarm blaring in his mind, to rediscover the sense of security and peace that had been lost during those three fateful days.
